meta.name: Oracle Certified Professional: Java SE 17 Developer (1Z0-829)
meta.notes: Initial release — Java SE 17 Developer (1Z0-829) core objectives: switch expressions, sealed classes, records, try-with-resources, Stream collectors, local-variable type inference (var), pattern matching for instanceof, text blocks, Optional, Map computeIfAbsent, and the Java Platform Module System.

options: A. Each arm needs an explicit break after the arrow to prevent fallthrough
B. The switch must include a default branch even when every enum constant is covered
C. When the case label uses ->, execution does not fall through to the next label
D. Multiple case labels on the same arm must be separated by semicolons
questions.explanation: Arrow-form switch labels (standardised in Java 14 and unchanged in 17) do not fall through to the next label, so no break is needed. Multiple labels on the same arm are separated by commas, not semicolons. When the selector expression is an enum and the switch is exhaustive over its constants (as here), a switch expression does not require a default branch — the compiler proves exhaustiveness at compile time. A switch statement using traditional colon-form labels still falls through unless break is used.

questions.question: Which statement about sealed classes and interfaces in Java 17 is CORRECT?
options: A. Every direct subclass of a sealed class must be declared final, sealed, or non-sealed
B. Any class in the same package as a sealed class may extend it without being permitted
C. Sealed types are restricted to top-level declarations and cannot be nested
D. A sealed interface may not be extended by any other interface
questions.explanation: A sealed class or interface restricts which types may extend or implement it via its permits clause, and each permitted direct subclass must itself be either final (no further extension), sealed (permits its own listed subclasses), or non-sealed (re-opens further extension). A class in the same package that is not listed in permits still gets a compile-time error, so package membership alone is not enough. Sealed types may be nested inside other types. A sealed interface may be extended by other interfaces provided they appear in the permits clause and comply with the same final/sealed/non-sealed rule.

questions.question: Which statement about Java 17 records is TRUE?
options: A. A record may declare additional non-static instance fields beyond its header components
B. A record is implicitly final and cannot extend another class
C. The compiler generates public setter methods for every record component
D. The developer cannot supply a canonical constructor to validate the components
questions.explanation: Records are implicitly final and implicitly extend java.lang.Record, so they cannot extend any other class (though they can implement interfaces). Records are restricted to the state declared in their header — additional instance fields are forbidden; static fields are allowed. The compiler generates accessor methods named after the components (e.g. name()), not JavaBean-style setters, and record instances are shallowly immutable. Developers may write a compact or full canonical constructor to validate or normalise incoming component values.

options: A. Only the first resource declared is auto-closed if an exception is thrown
B. Resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration
C. Resources declared in the try header must be marked with the explicit final keyword
D. A catch or finally block is mandatory when using try-with-resources
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes resources in the reverse order of their declaration — out is closed first, then in — whether or not an exception was thrown, and every resource declared in the header is closed (not only the first). Since Java 9, a resource may be declared elsewhere and referenced in the try header as long as it is effectively final; the explicit final keyword is not required. try-with-resources is a complete statement on its own, so neither catch nor finally is required.

options: A. A Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> with entries {false=[1, 3], true=[2, 4]}
B. A List<Integer> containing only the even numbers
C. A Map<Integer, Boolean> mapping each number to its parity
D. A Set<List<Integer>> containing two disjoint lists
questions.explanation: Collectors.partitioningBy(predicate) always returns a Map<Boolean, List<T>> with exactly two keys — true (elements matching the predicate) and false (the rest) — even when one bucket ends up empty. Collectors.groupingBy would use arbitrary key types drawn from the classifier, and Stream.filter would return only a filtered stream of matching elements, not the full partition. The keys here are Boolean (not Integer) and the wrapping collection is a List (not a Set).

questions.question: Which of the following uses of the var keyword is NOT permitted by the Java 17 compiler?
options: A. var list = new ArrayList<String>(); as a local variable declaration
B. var i = 0; inside the header of a for loop
C. var op = (int a, int b) -> a + b; as a local variable declaration
D. var name = "Alice"; inside the body of a static initialiser block
questions.explanation: A lambda expression has no standalone type — it needs an explicit target functional-interface type such as IntBinaryOperator — so var cannot be used as the declared type of a variable initialised with a lambda. var is permitted in any local variable declaration with an initialiser, including inside for and try-with-resources headers, method bodies, and static initialiser blocks. var is NOT allowed for fields, method parameters, method return types, or for local variables without an initialiser or with a null literal initialiser.

questions.question: Which statement about pattern matching for the instanceof operator in Java 17 is TRUE?
options: A. The pattern variable it introduces is visible everywhere in the enclosing method
B. It still requires an explicit cast on the object before the pattern variable can be used
C. It combines the type check and the cast, binding the object to a pattern variable when the test succeeds
D. It can be applied only to record types
questions.explanation: if (obj instanceof String s) performs the type check and, if it succeeds, binds obj (already cast to String) to the pattern variable s — the explicit cast previously needed after a plain instanceof check is gone. The pattern variable's scope is flow-scoped: it is visible only in the branches where the test is definitely true, not throughout the enclosing method. Pattern matching for instanceof applies to any reference type; record types get an additional feature called record patterns (a preview in Java 17), which is separate.

questions.question: Which statement about text blocks (a standard feature since Java 15, unchanged in Java 17) is CORRECT?
options: A. A text block may open with a triple-quote followed immediately by content on the same line
B. Incidental leading whitespace is stripped based on the least-indented non-blank line
C. Escape sequences such as \n and \t are ignored inside a text block
D. A text block always ends with an implicit trailing newline character
questions.explanation: A text block's incidental indentation is removed by finding the minimum leading whitespace among all non-blank lines (including the line containing the closing delimiter) and stripping that amount from every line — the re-indentation algorithm defined by JEP 378. The opening triple-quote must be followed by a line terminator; content cannot begin on the same line. Standard escape sequences (\n, \t, \", \\, etc.) are honoured inside a text block. A trailing newline is present only when a line terminator follows the last content line before the closing delimiter — placing the closing quotes at the end of the last content line omits it.

questions.question: Which expression safely returns the length of the String inside Optional<String> opt, yielding 0 when the Optional is empty?
options: A. opt.orElse("").length()
B. opt.map(String::length).orElseGet(0)
C. opt.get().length()
D. opt.ifPresent(s -> s.length())
questions.explanation: orElse supplies a fallback value when the Optional is empty, so opt.orElse("").length() yields the wrapped string's length or 0 for the empty-string fallback, with no NoSuchElementException risk. opt.get() throws NoSuchElementException when the Optional is empty. orElseGet takes a Supplier<T>, not a raw value — the correct form would be orElseGet(() -> 0) — so option B does not compile. ifPresent returns void: it consumes the value with a side-effecting Consumer and cannot return a length to the caller.

questions.question: Given Map<String, List<String>> map, which single call is the idiomatic Java 17 way to append "b" to the list stored under key "a", creating the list if the key is not yet present?
options: A. map.computeIfAbsent("a", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("b");
B. map.putIfAbsent("a", new ArrayList<>()).add("b");
C. map.getOrDefault("a", new ArrayList<>()).add("b");
D. map.merge("a", List.of("b"), List::addAll);
questions.explanation: computeIfAbsent returns the value now associated with the key — the freshly created ArrayList when the key was absent, or the existing list otherwise — so its return can be used directly to add("b"). putIfAbsent returns the previous value, which is null when the key was absent, causing a NullPointerException on the chained .add. getOrDefault returns the default list without storing it in the map, so the mutation is lost the moment the reference is dropped. List.of("b") is immutable and List::addAll does not have a signature compatible with Map.merge's BiFunction<V,V,V> that would produce a merged, mutable list here.

questions.question: In module-info.java, what is the difference between requires and requires transitive?
options: A. requires transitive additionally grants any module that reads mine an implicit read edge to the required module
B. requires transitive is mandatory whenever the required module itself reads any other module
C. Only requires transitive allows a module to use reflective access to the required module's non-public members
D. requires transitive is a synonym for requires static and only applies at compile time
questions.explanation: requires transitive M means: any other module that reads MY module also implicitly reads M. This is how a module re-exports a dependency as part of its own public API surface (for example, when its API returns types declared by M). Plain requires M gives MY module access to M but does not propagate that read edge to downstream consumers. requires static is a separate modifier that marks a compile-time-only dependency (optional at runtime). Reflective access into non-public members is controlled by opens (or opens ... to), not by requires.
